blocks.text: It should be noted that both עזניה oznija and פרס peres are taken by some for the griffin, and that accordingly both are rendered עוז uz or עוזא uza, a word that among the paraphrasts and the Talmudists means griffin. Thus in Jonathan's paraphrase עוזא uza stands for פרס peres, while in the Samaritan ࠏࠅࠆࠀ uza stands for ࠏࠆࠍࠉࠄ oznija. And in the Talmudic tractate Kelim, ch. 17, § 14, where vessels made מכנף העוז, from the wing of the uz, that is, of the griffin, are discussed, the Glossator has this: עוף הוא ששמו עזניה ורגילים היו לעשות כלים מכנף אותו העוז, It is a bird which (in the sacred text) is called oznija, from whose wings vessels used to be made. Here perhaps instead of מכנף miccanaph (from the wing) we should read מכף miccaph (from the sole). And shortly after, כף העוז מכל הכפים, The sole (of the bird) uz surpasses every other, instead of כנף העוז מכל הכנפים, The wing of the bird uz surpasses every wing. Sole, that is, foot and talon; for that is what כף caph means in birds. So Gen. VIII, 9. The dove found no rest לכף רגלה: and Erpenianus has لكف رجلها [li-kaff rijlihā] for the sole of her foot, that is, τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῆς [tois posin autēs], for her feet, as the Greeks have there. Moreover, they commonly say that vessels are made from the griffin's feet or talons, not from its wings. Damir, in the chapter On [col. 190] عنقا [ʿanqā] anka, or the Griffin: فيصنع من مخاليبها اقداح [II, 776] عظام للشرب [fa-yuṣnaʿ min makhālībihā aqdāḥ ʿiẓām li-l-shurb] And from its talons large drinking vessels are made. Gesner, on the griffin: John Mandeville writes that its talons are like the horns of an ox, from which cups of great value are made. And shortly after: I remember seeing at a goldsmith's in our city a smooth black horn, hooked at the top, almost as in chamois, perhaps three times as thick, whose rim the goldsmith was about to mount in silver, so that it might be used as a cup at table. It was perhaps the horn of some foreign ox, such as the one they call Indian, or of a buffalo. But he had received it as a griffin's talon. I shall adduce another testimony showing that עזניה oznija is the griffin in the opinion of the Hebrews. In the book בעל החיים, or On the Natures of Animals, which Calonymus translated from the Arabic of Abulsapha into Hebrew, the עזניה oznija, ruling far and wide over the birds of prey, summons them from every side and speaks thus in their council: הנה אני עם גודל גופי ואומץ כוחי ומהירות עופפותי עזבתי בתיהם וברחתי מהם אל האיים הרחוקים ואל ההרים הרמים והנשואים, I indeed, though vast in body, outstanding in strength and swift of wing, have left their (men's) dwellings and fled from them to remote islands and to steep and lofty mountains. Not very differently Maimonides on the peres and the oznija, in the tractate On Forbidden Foods, ch. 1, § 17: פרס ועזניה אינן מצויין בישוב אלא במדברות איי הים הרחוקות עד מאד שהן סוף הישוב, The Perez and the oznija are not found in the inhabited world (ἐν τῇ οἰκουμένῃ [en tē oikoumenē]), but in the most remote islands of the sea at the farthest edge of the world. It is obvious that this refers to the anca of the Arabs, or griffin, which they fable once lived among men in Arabia and fed on beasts and birds; but when it had once carried off children and even a bride, it was banished at the prayers of the Prophet Handala to an island most remote from human intercourse, from which it is forbidden to come out to betake itself to more cultivated places. Accordingly, for the Hebrew עזניה oznija one reads in the Arabic paraphrases, of Saadia as of others, العنقا [al-ʿanqā] alanka. And for this reason Aben Ezra is angry with Saadia for holding that God forbade הדבר שלא היה, a thing that does not exist. The Arabs themselves admit this. Among them is Alcamus, by whom العنقا [al-ʿanqā] alanka is defined with an elegant paronomasia as طاير معروف الاسم ومجهول الجسم [ṭāʾir maʿrūf al-ism wa-majhūl al-jism], a bird of known alism, that is, name, but unknown algism, that is, body. And the poet who says الجود والغول والعنقا ثلاثة اسما اشيا لم توجد ولم تكن [al-jūd wa-l-ghūl wa-l-ʿanqā thalātha asmā ashyā lam tūjad wa-lam takun] Liberality, and algol (or empusa) and alanca (or griffin) are three names of things that are not found and exist nowhere. But elsewhere I show that Saadia and the other paraphrasts who use this word can be excused, because, although anca is mostly the name of a fictitious bird, as griffins are for us, yet it sometimes also occurs for a real bird. But whatever they had in mind, this is certain: עזניה oznija in Moses signifies a real bird, and very probably it is the black eagle, which the Greeks call by the compound word μελαναίετον [melanaieton].
